ZLATTE: A Geometry-Aware, Learning-Free Framework for Language-Driven Trajectory Reshaping in Human-Robot Interaction

Junhui Huang Affiliation:  Junhui Huang Changsheng Li and Xingguang Duan are with the Beijing Institute of Technology (BIT). Affiliation: The authors are with the School of Computer Science, University of Nottingham, UK.    Yuhe Gong Affiliation: The authors are with the School of Computer Science, University of Nottingham, UK.    Changsheng Li Affiliation:  Junhui Huang Changsheng Li and Xingguang Duan are with the Beijing Institute of Technology (BIT).    Xingguang Duan Affiliation:  Junhui Huang Changsheng Li and Xingguang Duan are with the Beijing Institute of Technology (BIT).    Luis Figueredo Affiliation: The authors are with the School of Computer Science, University of Nottingham, UK. Abstract

We present ZLATTE, a geometry-aware, learning-free framework for language-driven trajectory reshaping in human-robot interaction. Unlike prior learning-based methods, ZLATTE leverages Vision-Language Models to register objects as geometric primitives and employs a Large Language Model to translate natural language instructions into explicit geometric and kinematic constraints. These constraints are integrated into a potential field optimization to adapt initial trajectories while preserving feasibility and safety. A multi-agent strategy further enhances robustness under complex or conflicting commands. Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that ZLATTE achieves smoother, safer, and more interpretable trajectory modifications compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

I Introduction

As robots transition from structured industrial environments to dynamic, human-centric spaces, the need for intuitive and seamless human-robot interaction (HRI) becomes paramount. A critical aspect of this interaction is enabling robots to adapt their movements in response to human preferences. The central challenge this work addresses is: given an initial, feasible trajectory, how can a robot modify its path to align with nuanced, natural language commands while respecting the physical and geometric constraints of its environment?

Traditional robotic paradigms, such as pre-programmed automation, planning-from-scratch algorithms like RRT* [1], and even Learning from Demonstration (LfD) [2], exhibit significant limitations in dynamic, human-centric environments. Pre-programmed robots lack the ability to adapt to new contexts, while planners that compute paths from scratch are often not reactive to on-the-fly changes. Although LfD allows non-experts to teach robots, it struggles with generalizing learned behaviors to novel situations and typically requires extensive data collection for each task. Language-driven trajectory modification emerges as a more flexible and powerful paradigm. By enabling robots to understand and respond to natural language commands, we move beyond rigid, pre-defined behaviors. So we propose ZLATTE, this approach allows users to intuitively convey nuanced, contextual adjustments, granting a level of adaptability and on-demand refinement, thereby bridging the gap between rigid robotic execution and the fluid demands of real-world human-robot collaboration.

Recent advances in foundation models, particularly Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like GPT [3] Deepseek [4], Gemini [5], SAM[6], offer powerful new tools to bridge the gap between environmental constraints, user semantics, and robot execution. To effectively act on a command, a robot must first ground the language in a precise understanding of its physical surroundings. Simply representing objects as abstract points is insufficient, as it can lead to unsafe or illogical movements, such as a trajectory penetrating an object’s volume. Our approach, therefore, begins by establishing a high-fidelity geometric representation of the scene. We leverage VLMs to not only identify objects but also to register their detailed shapes. Subsequently, built upon the strong semantic comprehension abilities of LLMs, we could easily interpret the user’s command, translating the abstract intent into concrete geometric constraints that can be applied to trajectories.

Starting from any geometrical planner (e.g. A*, RRT* [1], MPC [7]), which are concerned solely about obstacle avoidance and dynamics constraints, we propose a novel, learning-free framework that enables robots to reshape their trajectories in response to complex language instructions. Specifically, this paper makes the following contributions.

  • •

    Vision-based Geometric Registration: We propose a pipeline for automated geometric registration leveraging Vision-Language Models (VLMs) and foundation vision models.

  • •

    Geometric Constraints: By incorporating geometric constraints into the potential field, we achieve trajectory reshaping that considers the geometric features of objects.

  • •

    LLM-driven and Multi-Agent Reshaping: We introduce a Large Language Model (LLM) to translate natural language instructions into constraints and utilize a multi-agent system to enhance the success rate of complex, constrained tasks.

II Related Work

II-A Natural Language Interfaces for Robotic Interaction

A fundamental challenge in enabling intuitive human-robot interaction is grounding the rich semantics of natural language within the physical constraints of a robot’s environment. While non-expert users require flexible interfaces, historical approaches have struggled to bridge this semantic gap. Early methods were limited, either by confining users to rigid command structures [8] or employing complex probabilistic models that were difficult to scale [9, 10]. More recently, a dominant paradigm has emerged: using deep neural networks, including large-scale foundation models, to learn a direct, end-to-end mapping from language to robot actions [11, 12].

While subsequent research [13, 14, 15] has sought to mitigate these data requirements and improve generalization using large foundation models[16, 17], these approaches still demand extensive training. Furthermore, their fixed, post-training parameters limit their adaptability to new environments, and their reliance on a direct alignment between commands and objects often fails when interpreting complex user intent, leading to unpredictable results. This motivates a different paradigm: to enhance the reliability of intent recognition, using a Large Language Model to explicitly generate intermediate constraints for trajectory modification provides a more interpretable and controllable outcome.

II-B Geometry for Robotics

Geometry has long played a foundational role in robotics, enabling precise spatial reasoning necessary for motion planning, control, and environment interaction [18]. Geometric methods have been applied to the constraints in task and motion planning, where object modeling and spatial relationships are encoded through geometric predicates [19, 20, 21]. More specifically, differential geometric tools have facilitated the design of control strategies for systems with non-Euclidean configuration spaces, such as mobile manipulators and aerial robots [22]. Additionally, the use of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs), convex decomposition (such as GJK) [23, 24, 25], and mesh-based representations [26, 27, 28] in modern planning pipelines reflects the enduring utility of geometry in modeling complex environments [29]. However, the existing methods—including iterative approaches like GJK—are fundamentally limited in providing accurate and reliable closest point information, as they rely on abstract geometric proxies (e.g., simplices or bounding volumes) rather than directly modeling the continuous surface of the geometry surfaces. This often results in inefficient or imprecise calculation, particularly in complex environments.

More recently, a geometric modeling and distance computation based on geometric primitives are established [30]. They sufficiently calculate the distance based on different geometry fields and demonstrate their efficiency. However, they ignores the geometry feature extraction - the geometry shape of the objects are assumed to be known, which is usually not the case in reality. Thus, a trajectory adaptation methods with geometry feature attraction and obstacle modeling based on the visual information is necessary.

II-C Large Language Model for Robotics

Recent advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have significantly enhanced robotic capabilities in spatial understanding and high-level task planning. A prominent line of research involves end-to-end Visual-Language-Action (VLA) models, such as PaLM-E [31] and openVLA [32], which directly map multi-modal inputs to low-level robot actions through implicit latent representations. Other paradigms leverage LLMs as intermediate tools: Code-as-Policies [33] translates tasks into interpretable code that orchestrates predefined motion primitives, while works like Voxposer [34],RobotGPT [35] and Rekep [36] parse user intent into a sequence of API calls. In the domain of manipulation, systems such as VISO-Grasp [37] and ThinkGrasp [38] merge the spatial reasoning of VLMs with specialized models like GraspNet [39] to perform complex grasping in cluttered environments.

A common thread in these approaches is a focus holistic trajectory generation, often abstracting away the fine-grained geometric features of objects. In contrast, our work addresses the specific challenge of modifying complex trajectories according to nuanced user preferences. We leverage the spatial reasoning of foundation models to create an automated visual registration pipeline, yielding a geometric representation for objects. Concurrently, an LLM interprets complex user commands to generate a diverse set of initial conditions that drive a multi-agent system. This allows our method to robustly adapt complex trajectories, ensuring the final path is precisely aligned with the user’s intent.

III Approach

Our approach presents a comprehensive framework for modifying robot trajectories based on natural language commands, ensuring the final path is both compliant with user intent and kinematically feasible. The system’s core is a two-stage process: first, it builds a detailed geometric understanding of the environment, and second, it refines an initial trajectory according to user instructions. To achieve scene understanding, we introduce an automated pipeline that leverages a Vision Language Model, along with foundational vision models to register objects and their geometric properties.

For trajectory modification, a separate Large Language Model translates the user’s command into a set of soft constraints. These constraints are then integrated into a geometry potential field-based optimization that iteratively adjusts the trajectory. This method balances external forces derived from the user’s command and obstacle avoidance with internal forces that maintain the trajectory’s smoothness and integrity. To robustly handle complex or conflicting commands, we introduce a novel multi-agent system where different agents attempt to solve the constraints using varied strategies—such as parallel, sequential, or LLM-prioritized execution, thereby increasing the success rate for complex, multi-constraint tasks.

III-A Problem Definition

We define the original, normalized robot trajectory as ξo:[−1,1]→ℝ4\xi_{o}:[-1,1]\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{4}, which is discretized into a sequence of NN waypoints, represented as ξo={(xi,yi,zi,vi)}i=1N\xi_{o}=\{(x_{i},y_{i},z_{i},v_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}. Here, (xi,yi,zi)(x_{i},y_{i},z_{i}) are the spatial coordinates and viv_{i} denotes the scalar speed at the ii-th waypoint. This initial trajectory is assumed to be kinematically feasible, having been pre-calculated by a standard motion planning algorithm, yet it does not fully satisfy all task-level specifications. To complete the task, the system receives a natural language instruction from the user, denoted as Li​nL_{in}, which specifies the required correction (e.g., Li​nL_{in} = “Go slower when next to the fragile glasses”).

Let 𝒪={O1,…,OM}\mathcal{O}=\{O_{1},\dots,O_{M}\} be the set of MM objects in the environment. Each object is characterized by its corresponding geometry, which encapsulates its position, orientation, dimensions, and shape.Our objective is to formulate a function, ff, that maps the original trajectory ξo\xi_{o}, the user command Li​nL_{in}, and the set of objects 𝒪\mathcal{O} to a modified trajectory ξm​o​d\xi_{mod}.This mapping is expressed as:

ξm​o​d=f⁡(ξo,Li​n,𝒪)\xi_{mod}=f(\xi_{o},L_{in},\mathcal{O})

III-B VLM based Geometry Registration

To acquire geometric information from the scene, we constructed an automated pipeline based on GPT-4o and foundation vision models. To obtain more comprehensive geometric features and enhance robustness against occlusions, the pipeline utilizes two eye-to-hand RGB-D cameras. These cameras are stereo-calibrated to enable point cloud fusion, with the accuracy further refined using the Iterative Closest Point (ICP) algorithm [40]. Subsequently, a hand-eye calibration algorithm transforms the fused point cloud into the robot’s base coordinate frame. The pipeline leverages the visual reasoning capabilities of GPT-4o to identify the names of objects in the environment and their most closely corresponding geometric shapes.

For each identified object, we sequentially use Grounding-DINO[41] and Segment-Anything 2 [42] to acquire its mask from different viewpoints. Based on these masks, the object’s point cloud is segmented from each respective view. After fusing the segmented point clouds, we first perform outlier removal. Following this, the DBSCAN [43] clustering algorithm is applied to further extract the target object’s point cloud and filter out noise. Finally, a 3D Oriented Bounding Box (OBB) is generated from the cleaned point cloud. Based on this 3D OBB and the previously identified object shape, a corresponding geometric primitive is generated in the robot’s base coordinate system. Our proposed visual registration pipeline includes common shapes such as cubes, cylinders, spheres, and cones. Because geometric primitives like planes often exceed the camera’s field of view, we have excluded them from the automated registration process. However, we provide a convenient interface for their manual addition, which also enables support for plane-based geometric constraints for trajectory modification.

III-C Geometric Constraints

After registering geometric primitives for each obstacle, the corresponding closest points can be efficiently computed and updated based on Euclidean geometric relationships. Following the approach of [30], we represent obstacles using a set of canonical geometric primitives, including spheres, planes, conics, cylinders, and cuboids. The computation of the closest distance relies on the analytic formulation of each primitive in Euclidean space.

  • •

    For spheres, the closest point lies along the direction pointing from the sphere’s center to the robot, and the distance is given by the Euclidean distance between the robot and the sphere’s center, minus the sphere’s radius.

  • •

    For planes, the closest point is determined by the orthogonal projection of the robot onto the plane. If the projected point lies within the finite extent of the plane, the closest distance is the perpendicular (normal) distance. Otherwise, the closest point is taken to be on the nearest edge of the plane boundary, and the distance is computed accordingly using a point-to-line segment formulation.

  • •

    For conics and cylinders, the closest point is derived based on the projection onto the curved surface. This involves identifying the closest generatrix (surface line), typically by projecting the robot position onto the main axis of the shape and determining the nearest point on the corresponding surface line.

  • •

    For conics and cylinders, the closest point is derived based on the projection onto the curved surface. This involves identifying the closest generatrix (surface line), typically by moving the main axis of the shape along the robot direction to the surface line.

  • •

    For cuboids, the closest distance is obtained by evaluating the shortest distance from the robot to the six planes.

III-D Constraint Generation and Satisfaction

We employ a separate Large Language Model (LLM) for user intent understanding, which translates natural language commands into corresponding constraints. These constraints include: the modification type, specifying the desired nature of the trajectory reshaping; the direction of the modification; and its intensity. For object-based trajectory modification tasks, the LLM aligns the user’s instructions with the objects identified through visual registration. In scenarios involving multiple instructions, the LLM is also tasked with generating different constraint sequences and additional importance parameters, which are determined based on the significance and fragility of the involved objects.

After obtaining the constraints, we use a potential field-based method to iteratively refine the trajectory. The refinement process seeks to minimize an implicit objective function by applying a composite force field to each waypoint. This field comprises internal forces that preserve geometric properties like segment length and curvature, an external force that couples the trajectory to constraints generated from user commands and handles obstacle avoidance—wherein obstacle avoidance is achieved by adding a repulsive force with a very small range of influence to each object in the scene—and a regularization force that penalizes deviation from the initial path. The iterative application of these forces guides the trajectory toward a locally optimal configuration.

The position of each waypoint is influenced by a total force vector 𝐅j,total\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{total}},At any iteration ii, the total force on waypoint is given by:

𝐅j,total(i)=𝐅j,wp(i)+𝐅j,ang(i)+𝐅j,ext(i)+𝐅j,self(i)\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{total}}^{(i)}=\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{wp}}^{(i)}+\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{ang}}^{(i)}+\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{ext}}^{(i)}+\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{self}}^{(i)}

Each component of this force field is described below. Internal Spring ForceTo maintain the intrinsic length of the trajectory segments, an internal spring-like force is introduced.

𝐟j,𝐰𝐩(i)=k⁡(‖𝐰j+1(i)−𝐰j(i)‖−‖𝐰j+1(0)−𝐰j(0)‖)​𝐰j+1(i)−𝐰j(i)‖𝐰j+1(i)−𝐰j(i)‖\mathbf{f}_{j,\mathbf{wp}}^{(i)}=k\left(\|\mathbf{w}_{j+1}^{(i)}-\mathbf{w}_{j}^{(i)}\|-\|\mathbf{w}_{j+1}^{(0)}-\mathbf{w}_{j}^{(0)}\|\right)\frac{\mathbf{w}_{j+1}^{(i)}-\mathbf{w}_{j}^{(i)}}{\|\mathbf{w}_{j+1}^{(i)}-\mathbf{w}_{j}^{(i)}\|}
𝐅j,wp(i)=𝐟j−1,wp(i)−𝐟j,wp(i)\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{wp}}^{(i)}=\mathbf{f}_{j-1,\mathrm{wp}}^{(i)}-\mathbf{f}_{j,\mathrm{wp}}^{(i)}

where kk is is a scalar stiffness coefficient. wiw_{i} is the position of waypoints.

Curvature Regularization Force:To ensure smoothness, a force that regularizes the trajectory’s curvature is applied.

𝐜j(i)=(𝐰j+2(i)−𝐰j+1(i)2)−(𝐰j+1(i)−𝐰j(i)2)\mathbf{c}_{j}^{(i)}=\left(\frac{\mathbf{w}_{j+2}^{(i)}-\mathbf{w}_{j+1}^{(i)}}{2}\right)-\left(\frac{\mathbf{w}_{j+1}^{(i)}-\mathbf{w}_{j}^{(i)}}{2}\right)

where kangk_{\mathrm{ang}} is the angular stiffness coefficient. External Constraint Force This force is derived from one or more cost functions, 𝒢\mathcal{G}, which encode information about obstacles, object information 𝒪\mathcal{O}, and user intention Li​nL_{in}.

𝐅j,ext(i)=w⋅𝒢⁡(𝐰j(i),𝒪,Li​n)\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{ext}}^{(i)}=w\cdot\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{w}_{j}^{(i)},\mathcal{O},L_{in})

𝐅j,self(i)=wself​(𝐰j(i)−𝐰j(0))\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{self}}^{(i)}=w_{\mathrm{self}}\left(\mathbf{w}_{j}^{(i)}-\mathbf{w}_{j}^{(0)}\right)

where wselfw_{\mathrm{self}} the adherence weighting factor. At each iteration ii, the position of every waypoint is updated based on the total calculated force.

ξj(i+1)=ξj(i)+η⋅𝐅j,total(i)\mathbf{\xi}_{j}^{(i+1)}=\mathbf{\xi}_{j}^{(i)}+\eta\cdot\mathbf{F}_{j,\mathrm{total}}^{(i)}

where η\eta is a learning rate or step-size parameter. This iterative process is repeated for a fixed number of steps to get the modified trajectory.

III-E Multi-agent system

To address scenarios involving multiple, concurrent instructions of the same type, which may conflict and prevent the target constraints from being achieved, we have designed a multi-agent system composed of four distinct agents:i) Parallel Agent: Treats all target instructions as equal, applying all corresponding potential fields simultaneously. ii) Sequential Agent: Executes all instructions sequentially in the order provided by the user, modifying the trajectory iteratively. iii) Parallel Agent with Priority: A parallel agent that utilizes a Large Language Model (LLM) to reorder user instructions based on the importance and fragility of the involved objects. iv) Parallel Agent with Importance: A parallel agent that receives an additional ’intensity’ input for each constraint, with the value determined by the LLM based on object importance and fragility.

In our pipeline, constraints generated by the LLM are first sent to an Initial Planner, which translates them into corresponding potential fields. These are then passed to the Agents to generate modified trajectories. The resulting trajectories are evaluated by an Observer that performs constraint checks based on the original LLM output. If none of the generated trajectories satisfy the user’s instructions, a Refinement Planner initiates an adjustment process. Specifically, if individual constraints can be met but the overall objective fails, we adjust the corresponding intensity, importance, and priority parameters. If, however, a single constraint cannot be satisfied at all, we infer that the object is too far from the trajectory in the default setting and proceed to expand the influence range of that object’s potential field.The refinement process iterates for a specified number of cycles or until all constraints are satisfied.

IV Experiments

We c

IV-A Dataset

To construct our dataset, we adopt the synthetic data generation methodology proposed in [11], [12]. Each data sample comprises three primary components: an initial trajectory ξo\xi_{o}, a natural language command Li​nL_{in}, and a set of environmental objects 𝒪={O1,…,OM}\mathcal{O}=\{O_{1},\dots,O_{M}\}, where each object is described by its pose (position and orientation) and corresponding geometry. Initial trajectories are generated by randomly sampling waypoints within the workspace and subsequently applying spline interpolation to ensure a smooth path. For the language commands, we utilize the three trajectory modification types introduced in [50]: i) absolute Cartesian adjustments (e.g., “go more to the right”), ii) speed modifications (e.g., “slow down when next to the table”), and iii) object-relative positional changes (e.g., “move closer to the chair”).

In total, we curated three distinct types of datasets based on this approach. The first is a single-command dataset, which is analogous to the configuration used in LATTE. Additionally, we assembled a multi-command dataset. Finally, to specifically evaluate the model’s capability in handling complex constraints, we created a third dataset where each language input consists of multiple, concatenated instructions for trajectory modification.

IV-B Simulation Results and Analysis

We evaluate our method in several simulated scenarios, validating the model’s performance on three distinct datasets. The core functionality of our trajectory adaptation method is illustrated in Fig. 2. In this representative scenario, given an initial trajectory that traverses near a set of objects and a language command indicating the desired modification (e.g., moving farther from or closer to an object, or going faster or slower in its vicinity), our model predicts a revised trajectory that adheres to the user’s intent. The generated trajectories demonstrate that our model successfully incorporates both spatial modifications and the specified changes to the speed profile.

compare with latte: We benchmarked our method against the previous state-of-the-art model, LATTE, on two standard datasets: a single-user-command dataset, which is identical to the one used in the original LATTE study, and a multi-user-command dataset, which can be considered an extension of the former. Since LATTE does not account for object geometry, we provided it with the centroid of our registered geometry as the object’s pose and applied the same normalization methods as described in their paper to ensure output consistency.

As illustrated in Fig. 3 compared to the learning-based LATTE model, our learning-free method produces significantly smoother output trajectories. By explicitly invoking constraints, our approach guarantees that the optimization objectives are met. This is particularly evident in the multi-command scenario, where our model maintains stable and predictable trajectory modifications without conflating different user intentions, demonstrating a clear advantage over the previous method.

compare with geo: To better demonstrate the operational mechanism of our geometry-based potential field for trajectory modification, we provide visualizations of the geometric shapes, the trajectory, and the corresponding closest points between them. Each shape defines a potential field with a finite range of influence; beyond this range, it exerts no force on the trajectory, and no closest points are computed. As depicted in Fig. 4, a series of closest points forms on the object’s surface nearest to the trajectory, which is corresponding to different waypoints and demonstrates that our geometry-based potential field effectively captures the object’s detailed geometric information. In contrast, approaches that disregard geometry approximate an object using only its center point. Conventional methods, particularly in real-world applications, often use the centroid of a 2D bounding box for this purpose. Such a point is often detached from and suspended above the actual object surface, which can introduce significant errors during trajectory modification.

We conducted comparative experiments between our geometry-based approach and a point-based method, where the latter used the centroid of the 3D bounding box from visual registration as the object’s representation. To ensure a fair comparison, both methods were driven by the same LLM to guarantee accuracy in constraint generation. As shown in the left of Fig. 5, when instructed to move closer to an object, the point-based method generates a trajectory that penetrates the object’s volume—an infeasible and hazardous outcome in a real-world setting. In contrast, our geometry-based method, by calculating closest points on the object’s surface, enables the trajectory to move proximate to the object without causing a collision. Similarly, the right of the figure illustrates a speed modification task. When commanded to accelerate while near a table, the point-based method only increases the speed in the immediate vicinity of the table’s centroid. Our geometry-based approach, however, correctly applies the speed change throughout the entire region of influence defined by the table’s geometry. These results underscore the critical importance of incorporating geometric information for accurate and safe trajectory modification.

compare with multi-agent To validate the effectiveness of our proposed multi-agent system, we conducted challenging trajectory modification tasks. The constraints generated by the LLM are used to formulate corresponding checks. These include i) distance check, which evaluates the average distance of the five trajectory points closest to the object before and after the modification; ii) Cartesian check, which verifies the trajectory’s displacement along a specified direction; and iii) speed check, which examines the velocity changes for the five closest points. An agent is considered successful if it satisfies all its assigned constraint checks. We deployed four agents simultaneously, and the multi-agent system is deemed successful if at least one agent succeeds. The experiment consisted of one initial generation round under default conditions, followed by three rounds of self-correction with feedback, during which we recorded the success rate of each agent per round.

Fig. 6 shows the success rate of each agent in the first and final rounds. Every agent demonstrates a notable improvement, proving the effectiveness of our multi-round refinement strategy. Fig. 7 presents the per-round success rates of the single-agent and multi-agent systems. The single-agent approach is the default parallel agent. The results indicate that the multi-agent system achieves a higher success rate than the single-agent system, and its performance also surpasses that of the best-performing individual agent. This validates the efficacy of our multi-agent system design. However, it is also observed that the success rate of the multi-agent system begins to plateau after the third round. This is attributed to the high complexity of some tasks, where satisfying one constraint can lead to the violation of another.

IV-C Real-World Experiments

real world setup: We deployed our approach in real-world experiments using a 7-DOF Franka Emika Panda robot equipped with a claw gripper. A computer equipped with an Intel i9-14900K CPU and an NVIDIA RTX 4060 GPU was used to deploy the arm’s low-level controller and our model. Two Realsense D435 RGB-D cameras were utilized to provide dual-viewpoint images and point clouds. The GPT-4o model for visual registration and LLM for constraint generation were accessed via its API service, while the LLM could be either GPT-4o or the more cost-effective DeepSeek-V3 model. The Grounding-DINO and Segment Anything2 models were deployed locally.

Visual registration in real-world scenarios:During the visual registration stage, we set the threshold for the ICP registration algorithm to 0.02m and selected mask segments with a confidence score higher than 0.99. To preprocess the segmented point cloud of objects, we first applied statistical outlier removal using 20 nearest neighbors and a standard deviation ratio of 1.0 to eliminate noise. Subsequently, density-based clustering was performed with a neighborhood radius of 0.15 meters and a minimum of 15 points required to form a cluster.

We placed random objects in a real-world robotic scene to test our visual registration pipeline, as illustrated in Figure X. The left panel shows the 3D Oriented Bounding Boxes (OBBs) of the objects, which are generated based on their masks and point clouds. The right panel displays the corresponding geometric primitives generated from the identified object shapes and their 3D OBBs. Through the results of hand-eye calibration, these primitives have been transformed into the robot’s base coordinate frame, thereby completing the scene perception .

Real world trajectory execuation For practical implementation in real-world applications, both the input trajectory and the geometry of environmental objects are first normalized to ensure uniformity in the scale of modifications. The original trajectory is then downsampled to accelerate the computation of the modification module. After the modification is complete, interpolation and inverse normalization are applied to reconstruct the trajectory for execution. Once this final path is obtained, the user can employ any suitable inverse kinematics algorithm to compute the corresponding joint-space trajectories for the robot.

V Conclusion

In this work, we introduced a learning-free framework that enables robots to reshape their trajectories in response to complex natural language commands. Our approach leverages VLM for automated geometric registration and utilizes LLM to translate user intent into actionable potential field forces. We conducted a comprehensive set of experiments, demonstrating our method’s superior performance in safety and accuracy against traditional point-based approaches and its enhanced stability compared to state-of-the-art learning-based models. Additionally, real-world and simulated results validate the necessity of our multi-agent system for robustly handling multi-constraint tasks and underscore the critical role of detailed geometry in achieving safe and intuitive human-robot interaction.

There’s still work to explore in the future. A primary limitation is the potential mismatch between the user’s perceived ”importance” of a command and the LLM’s interpretation; however, we found this often introduces a beneficial strategic diversity that aids our multi-agent system in finding a solution. Additionally, our system currently approximates each object with a single geometric primitive, which can limit precision for complex shapes. Future work could address this by representing objects as a composition of multiple geometries to achieve a higher-fidelity fit for more intricate and safer interactions.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
